title: America's Nuclear Industry Comes Courting — and India Has the Law, the Land, and the Ambition to Say Yes
excerpt: A high-level US delegation met Indian officials to discuss small modular reactors, the SHANTI Act, and a nuclear expansion plan that could reshape both countries' energy futures.
body:
A delegation of senior executives from the Nuclear Energy Institute and the US-India Strategic Partnership Forum sat down with India's Minister of State for Science and Technology, Dr Jitendra Singh, in New Delhi this week to discuss something that would have been unthinkable a generation ago: American private companies building nuclear reactors on Indian soil.

The meeting covered ground that spans the full spectrum of civil nuclear cooperation — from the long-delayed Westinghouse AP1000 project at Kovvada in Andhra Pradesh to advanced small modular reactors, micro-reactors, AI-enabled safety systems, and even the LIGO-India gravitational wave observatory. But the centrepiece of the conversation was India's ambition to scale its nuclear capacity from a modest 8.8 gigawatts today to an extraordinary 100 gigawatts by 2047, and the small modular reactors that could make the arithmetic possible.

## The SMR Bet

Small modular reactors are nuclear power plants designed to be built in factories and shipped to sites, rather than constructed from scratch over a decade the way traditional large reactors are. They generate between 50 and 300 megawatts each — a fraction of a conventional reactor's output — but their modularity means they can be deployed faster, scaled incrementally, and placed in locations where a full-sized plant would never fit: dense urban areas, remote industrial zones, or the grounds of decommissioned coal plants.

India has allocated nearly Rs 20,000 crore (roughly $2.4 billion) to SMR development under its Nuclear Energy Mission. The Bhabha Atomic Research Centre is working on indigenous designs including the BSMR-200 (220 megawatts) and a smaller SMR-55, while the government has signalled it wants foreign technology and capital to accelerate the timeline. Five SMRs are planned by 2033, with the technology eventually serving captive power generation for industry, data centres, and areas without grid connections.

The US has a clear commercial interest. In January 2026, the Department of Energy authorised Holtec International — a New Jersey-based nuclear technology company — to transfer its SMR-300 reactor design to India under the bilateral 123 Agreement. Three Indian firms have been designated as eligible partners: Larsen & Toubro, Tata Consulting Engineers, and Holtec Asia. The authorisation is valid for ten years and allows joint design, engineering, and eventually manufacturing of reactor components in India.

## The SHANTI Act Changes the Game

What makes this moment different from previous rounds of India-US nuclear diplomacy — which have a long history of ambitious announcements followed by glacial execution — is the SHANTI Act of 2025. The legislation, enacted by Parliament last year, opens India's nuclear sector to private and foreign participation for the first time, dismantling a state monopoly that has governed atomic energy since independence.

Dr Singh told the delegation that the implementation framework under the Act is being finalised, and that the reform is expected to create "a more enabling ecosystem for investment, industrial collaboration, manufacturing partnerships and technology cooperation." For American companies that have spent years circling the Indian market without a clear entry point, the SHANTI Act is the door they have been waiting for.

Tata Power has already begun advancing SMR projects with the Nuclear Power Corporation of India, with land acquisition underway in Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, and Odisha. Project reports are expected within six months, with regulatory approvals to follow.

## Beyond Reactors

The discussions extended well beyond power generation. The two sides reviewed cooperation in hydrogen production, rare earth processing, and high-intensity superconducting proton accelerators through partnerships with Fermilab. The LIGO-India project — a Rs 2,600 crore gravitational wave observatory being jointly implemented by India's Department of Atomic Energy, Department of Science and Technology, and the US-based LIGO Laboratory — was described as one of the most significant examples of advanced scientific collaboration between the two countries.

The TRUST Initiative, launched during the Modi-Trump meeting in February 2025, provides the overarching framework. It covers trusted technology partnerships, resilient supply chains, and innovation ecosystems across AI, semiconductors, biotechnology, quantum computing, and energy — a scope that makes nuclear cooperation one component of a much broader strategic alignment.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, particularly the large community of Indian-American engineers and scientists working in the US nuclear industry, the opening of India's nuclear sector represents both an opportunity and a test. The 123 Agreement removed the legal barriers to cooperation; the SHANTI Act removed the structural ones. What remains is the execution challenge: navigating India's regulatory complexity, managing the public anxieties that surround nuclear energy everywhere, and building the supply chain infrastructure that SMRs require.

India's nuclear ambitions also sit at the intersection of several forces the diaspora tracks closely: the country's energy security needs as crude oil prices remain elevated above $110 a barrel, the global AI boom's voracious appetite for reliable power (data centres alone could consume 8-10 per cent of India's electricity by 2035), and the geopolitical competition for clean energy leadership between the US and China.

If the SMR timeline holds — five units by 2033, scaled deployment thereafter — India could emerge as one of the world's largest markets for modular nuclear technology within a decade. For NRIs in energy, engineering, and technology, that is a professional landscape worth watching, and potentially, returning to.
